slides.n: Every time a student in Bhimber sends a WhatsApp voice note, checks a result on a board website or prints an assignment at a photocopy shop, an ICT system is at work. Information and Communication Technology (ICT) is the combination of devices, programs and networks that let people create, store, process, share and receive information. Computer science studies how these systems are built; ICT as a General Education subject focuses on using them well. This first lecture gives you the vocabulary that the rest of the course depends on: once you can name the parts of an ICT system, you can reason about why a file will not open, why the internet is slow in the lab, or where your photos are actually kept.

b: Data: raw facts (numbers, words, readings) without context.
Information: data that has been organised and given meaning.
IT focuses on computing; ICT adds telecommunication and broadcasting.
The information processing cycle: Input → Process → Output → Store → Communicate.
slides.n: ICT joins three ideas. Information is processed, meaningful data: a list of marks is data, but ‘Ali got the highest marks in Class 9’ is information. Communication is the transfer of that information between people or machines, by text, voice, image or video. Technology is the set of tools that makes the first two fast and cheap. ICT is wider than IT (Information Technology) because it also includes telecommunication: mobile networks, radio, television and the internet. An ICT system always follows the same cycle: input, processing, output, storage, and often communication to another system.
slides.v: Diagram: The information processing cycle

b: Input: keyboard, mouse, touch screen, scanner, microphone, webcam, barcode reader.
Processing: CPU (the ‘brain’), GPU for graphics, RAM as short-term working memory.
Output: monitor, printer, speakers, projector.
Storage: hard disk (HDD), solid-state drive (SSD), USB flash drive, memory card.
Communication: network card, Wi-Fi router, modem, mobile radio.
slides.n: Hardware is any part of an ICT system you can touch. It is easiest to understand by the job each device does in the processing cycle. Input devices bring data in, the processor (CPU) works on it using fast temporary memory (RAM), output devices show or print results, storage devices keep data when the power is off, and communication devices connect the system to others. A smartphone contains all five groups in one body: touch screen and camera (input), processor and RAM (processing), screen and speaker (output), internal flash storage (storage) and Wi-Fi, 4G and Bluetooth radios (communication).

b: System software: operating systems, drivers, utilities.
Application software: word processors, spreadsheets, browsers, apps.
Licensing types: proprietary, freeware, open source, subscription (Microsoft 365).
Without an operating system, application software cannot run.
slides.n: Software is the set of instructions that tells hardware what to do. System software manages the machine itself: the operating system (Windows, Android, macOS, Linux, iOS) controls files, memory, devices and users, while utility programs such as antivirus, backup and disk cleanup keep it healthy. Application software helps the user complete a task: Word for documents, Excel for calculations, Chrome for browsing, JazzCash for payments. Device drivers are small pieces of system software that let the operating system talk to a specific printer, scanner or graphics card. Software can be proprietary (Microsoft Office, paid licence), free (Google Docs, free to use but owned by a company) or open source (LibreOffice, source code anyone can study).

b: PAN: around one person (Bluetooth).
LAN: one building or campus, high speed, privately owned.
MAN: one city, for example a cable operator’s network.
WAN: many cities or countries, often leased lines.
Internet: the global network of networks using TCP/IP.
slides.n: A network is two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources such as a printer or an internet connection. Networks are grouped mainly by the area they cover. A Personal Area Network (PAN) links devices around one person, such as earbuds connected by Bluetooth. A Local Area Network (LAN) covers one building or campus, like the computer lab of a school, and is usually owned by that organisation. A Metropolitan Area Network (MAN) covers a city. A Wide Area Network (WAN) connects sites across cities or countries, such as a bank linking all its branches. The internet is the largest WAN: a global network of networks that uses common rules called protocols (TCP/IP). Devices connect by cable (Ethernet, fibre) or wirelessly (Wi-Fi, 4G/5G).

b: Primary memory: RAM (volatile, fast) and ROM (non-volatile, holds start-up instructions).
Secondary storage: HDD, SSD, USB, memory card (non-volatile).
Cloud storage: provider servers reached over the internet.
Typical sizes: a photo about 3 MB, a song about 5 MB, an HD film about 2 GB.
slides.n: Storage keeps data when the power is switched off. Local storage is inside or attached to your own device: the hard disk of a laptop, the phone’s internal memory or a USB drive. It works without internet and you control it physically, but it can be lost, stolen or damaged. Cloud storage keeps your files on servers owned by a provider such as Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive or Dropbox, and you reach them through the internet. It can be opened from any device and makes sharing easy, but it needs an internet connection and depends on a strong account password. RAM is not storage in this sense: it is volatile and loses its content when power is lost. Storage is measured in bytes: 1 KB = 1,024 bytes, 1 MB = 1,024 KB, 1 GB = 1,024 MB, 1 TB = 1,024 GB.

b: CPU: Central Processing Unit; carries out instructions and calculations.
RAM: Random Access Memory; fast temporary memory that is cleared when power is off.
Operating system: System software that manages hardware, files and applications.
Device driver: Software that lets the operating system control a specific device.
Protocol: An agreed set of rules for communication, such as TCP/IP or HTTP.
Bandwidth: The amount of data a connection can carry per second, measured in Mbps.

Network – Two or more connected devices that share data and resources.

slides.n: In Lecture 1 we looked inside an ICT system. Now we step back and ask where these systems are used and where they are going. Almost every sector in Pakistan has been reshaped by ICT in the last fifteen years: students submit assignments on Google Classroom, shopkeepers accept Easypaisa, patients book doctors on Marham and citizens verify property records online. At the same time, emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things are moving from research labs into ordinary phones and homes. Understanding this scope helps you choose a career, spot opportunities for local businesses and recognise the risks that come with new technology.

b: Online classes and recorded lectures
Learning Management Systems (Classroom, Moodle, Canvas)
Digital libraries and e-books

slides.n: ICT changes how students learn and how institutions manage teaching. Learning Management Systems such as Google Classroom and Moodle distribute material and collect assignments. Video lectures, digital libraries and online courses let a student in Bhimber learn from teachers anywhere in the world. Administration also depends on ICT: admissions, fee challans, attendance and results are increasingly handled online. The Higher Education Commission’s digital library gives university students access to research journals that would otherwise be unaffordable.

b: E-commerce and online marketplaces

Freelancing and remote work
slides.n: Businesses use ICT to sell, manage and communicate. Point-of-sale systems record every sale and update stock automatically. Spreadsheets and accounting software track income and expenses. Social media pages and WhatsApp Business let a small shop reach customers without paying for a physical advertisement. E-commerce platforms such as Daraz allow a seller in a small city to deliver across Pakistan. Freelancing platforms have made Pakistan one of the largest sources of online freelancers, with young people earning from graphic design, writing and programming.

b: NADRA identity and verification
FBR IRIS online tax filing
Pakistan Citizen’s Portal for complaints
Online land records and licence verification
slides.n: E-governance means delivering government services and information through ICT. It reduces queues, paperwork and opportunities for bribery, because each step is recorded. In Pakistan, NADRA issues identity cards through a national database, FBR’s IRIS portal lets citizens file tax returns online, the Pakistan Citizen’s Portal allows complaints to be lodged and tracked from a phone, and many provinces offer online driving licence verification and land record services.

slides.h: ICT in healthcare and digital media
b: Electronic health records and digital X-ray
Telemedicine and online appointments
Online news, streaming and content creation
Digital advertising
slides.n: Hospitals use ICT for patient records, digital imaging, laboratory reports and appointment systems. Telemedicine connects patients in remote areas to doctors in big cities by video call. In digital media, news, entertainment and advertising have moved online: people now watch YouTube and stream dramas instead of only waiting for a TV schedule, and anyone with a phone can publish content. This brings opportunities for creators but also spreads misinformation quickly, a topic we return to in Lecture 12.

b: AI: chatbots, face unlock, translation, recommendations
IoT: smart meters, CCTV, smart irrigation
Cloud computing: SaaS (Google Docs), storage, rented servers
5G: higher speed, low latency, many connected devices
slides.n: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is software that performs tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as recognising speech, translating languages or recommending videos. Machine learning, a branch of AI, lets software learn patterns from data instead of following only fixed rules. The Internet of Things (IoT) connects everyday objects such as meters, cameras and water pumps to the internet so they can send data and be controlled remotely. Cloud computing provides computing power, storage and software over the internet on demand, so a small business can rent a server instead of buying one. 5G is the fifth generation of mobile networks, offering much higher speed and lower delay than 4G, which supports IoT devices and real-time video.

b: E-governance: Delivery of government services and information through ICT.
E-commerce: Buying and selling goods or services over the internet.
Artificial Intelligence: Software that performs tasks needing human-like intelligence.
Machine learning: A type of AI in which systems learn patterns from data.
IoT: Internet of Things: everyday objects connected to the internet.
SaaS: Software as a Service: applications used through a browser on subscription or free.

Emerging technology – A new technology that is developing quickly and expected to have a large social or economic effect. Cloud computing – On-demand delivery of computing resources such as storage, servers and software over the internet.

slides.n: Most students search the way they speak: they type a full question and click the first result. That works for simple facts, but university assignments need accurate, citable sources. A search engine is not a list of truths; it is a ranking of pages that its software predicts you want. This lecture explains what happens behind the search box, teaches the operators that turn a vague query into a precise one, and gives you a simple test to decide whether a page deserves to be in your assignment.

b: Crawl: discover pages by following links
Index: store words and their page locations
Rank: order results by relevance and quality signals
Ads are labelled ‘Sponsored’ and are paid for
slides.n: A search engine does three jobs. Crawling: automated programs called crawlers or spiders follow links from page to page and download their content. Indexing: the content is analysed and stored in a giant index, like the index at the back of a book, that records which words appear on which pages. Ranking: when you type a query, the engine searches its index and orders the matching pages using hundreds of signals such as relevance of words, quality of the site, links from other pages, your location and freshness. Results marked ‘Sponsored’ or ‘Ad’ are paid placements, not necessarily the best answers.

b: Identify 2–4 main concepts
Remove question words and filler
Add type words: study, report, statistics, pdf
Refine using terms found in good results
slides.n: Good searching begins with good keywords. Remove filler words, keep the key concepts and add a word that describes the type of source you need. Instead of ‘what are the effects of mobile phones on students in Pakistan’, search ‘mobile phone use academic performance Pakistan study’. Use specific terms (‘literacy rate’ rather than ‘education level’), try synonyms when results are poor and add a year for recent data. Searching is iterative: read the first results, learn the correct terminology they use, then refine your query.

b: “exact phrase”
jaguar -car (exclude)
site:gov.pk or site:hec.gov.pk
filetype:pdf / filetype:pptx
Matric OR SSC
intitle:syllabus
slides.n: Operators are symbols or words that give the search engine exact instructions. Quotation marks search for an exact phrase. A minus sign excludes a word. site: limits results to one website or domain type, such as site:gov.pk for Pakistani government pages or site:edu.pk for universities. filetype: finds a specific format such as PDF or PPTX. OR (in capitals) finds either term. intitle: requires a word in the page title. Operators can be combined: “literacy rate” site:pbs.gov.pk filetype:pdf.

b: Currency – date
Relevance – fit to your question
Authority – author and organisation
Accuracy – evidence and references
Purpose – inform, sell or persuade?
slides.n: Before using a source, check five things. Currency: when was it published or updated, and is that recent enough for your topic? Relevance: does it answer your question at the right level? Authority: who wrote it, and what are their qualifications or organisation? Accuracy: is it supported by evidence, data or references, and do other reliable sources agree? Purpose: is it written to inform, or to sell, persuade or entertain? Official domains such as .gov.pk and .edu.pk, peer-reviewed journals and recognised news organisations are usually more reliable than anonymous blogs, forums or social media posts.

Bing: built into Edge and Windows
Google Scholar: research papers and citations

AI answers must be verified

slides.n: WhatsApp is perfect for friends, but universities, employers and government offices still communicate formally by email. Your first contact with a teacher about a missed quiz, an application for an internship or a complaint to a department will usually be an email, and its tone will shape how people see you. Video conferencing has also become part of normal study and work since online classes became common. This lecture teaches the tools and, more importantly, the manners of professional digital communication.

b: Address = username @ domain
SMTP sends mail; IMAP/POP3 receive it
Webmail (Gmail in browser) vs client (Outlook app)
Asynchronous: a permanent written record
slides.n: An email address has two parts separated by @: the user name and the domain, for example ali.khan@gmail.com or registrar@uob.edu.pk. When you click Send, your email client (Gmail, Outlook) passes the message to your provider’s outgoing mail server using the SMTP protocol. That server finds the recipient’s mail server from the domain name and delivers it. The recipient’s app then downloads or displays it using IMAP or POP3. Email is asynchronous: the receiver does not need to be online at the same moment, which makes it ideal for formal records.
slides.v: Diagram: Path of an email

b: To: main recipient who must act
CC: informed, visible to all
BCC: hidden recipients, protects privacy
Reply vs Reply all vs Forward
Attachments: clear names, PDF, under 25 MB
slides.n: To is for the main person who must read and act on the email. CC (carbon copy) is for people who should be kept informed; everyone can see who was CC’d. BCC (blind carbon copy) hides recipients from each other, which protects privacy when emailing a large group, such as a teacher writing to all parents. Attachments add files; keep them small (Gmail limits attachments to 25 MB and offers a Drive link for larger files), name them clearly such as Assignment2_AliKhan.pdf and prefer PDF so formatting does not change. Reply answers only the sender; Reply all answers everyone in To and CC, so use it carefully. Forward sends the message to someone new.

b: Subject
Greeting
Opening: identity and purpose
Body: details in short paragraphs
Closing request or thanks
Signature: name, roll no., department, phone
slides.n: A formal email has six parts. Subject line: short and specific, such as ‘Request for leave on 12 March – BSCS Section A’. Greeting: ‘Dear Sir/Madam’, ‘Dear Dr. Ahmed’ or ‘Respected Ma’am’. Opening line: who you are and why you are writing. Body: the details in short paragraphs, with dates and reference numbers. Closing: a polite request or thanks, such as ‘I would be grateful for your consideration.’ Signature: full name, roll number or designation, department and contact number. Avoid SMS language, all capital letters, emojis and slang in formal emails.

b: Proofread; check attachments
Professional address and tone
Labels, folders, archive
Recognise phishing: urgency, odd sender, suspicious links
slides.n: Reply within one or two working days, proofread before sending and check that attachments are actually attached. Do not forward chain messages. Use a professional address, ideally firstname.lastname rather than a nickname. Organise your inbox with labels or folders and archive old messages. Be alert to phishing: emails that pretend to be from a bank, university or courier and ask you to click a link or share a password or OTP. Check the sender’s real address, hover over links before clicking and never share a PIN or OTP by email.

slides.n: Video meetings are synchronous: everyone joins at the same time. Google Meet works in a browser with a Google account and integrates with Google Calendar and Classroom. Microsoft Teams combines chat, meetings and file sharing and is common in universities that use Microsoft 365. Zoom is widely used for webinars and large classes. All three support screen sharing, chat, raising a hand, recording (with permission) and breakout rooms in some plans. Good meeting etiquette: join on time, keep the microphone muted when not speaking, use a real name, turn the camera on when asked, use the chat for questions and stay focused.

slides.n: A word processor is the tool you will use most often at university: for assignments, lab reports, project documentation, applications and your CV. Most students use Word like a typewriter, pressing Enter repeatedly to move to a new page and making headings bold by hand. That makes documents hard to edit and impossible to navigate. This lecture shows how professionals work: they let styles control the appearance, let the software number pages and build the contents table, and use collaboration features so a group can work on one file without emailing versions back and forth.

b: Character: font, size, bold, italic, colour
Paragraph: alignment, spacing, indentation, lists
Page: margins, orientation, size (A4 in Pakistan)
Format Painter copies formatting quickly
slides.n: Microsoft Word is a desktop application, part of Microsoft Office or Microsoft 365, and also runs in a browser as Word for the web. Google Docs runs in a browser, saves automatically to Google Drive and is free with a Google account. Both handle the same core tasks. Character formatting changes text: font, size, bold, italic, underline, colour. Paragraph formatting changes whole paragraphs: alignment (left, centre, right, justify), line spacing, spacing before and after, indentation, bullets and numbering. For academic work, a clean font such as Calibri, Times New Roman or Arial at 11–12 point with 1.15–1.5 line spacing is standard.

b: Apply styles from Home → Styles (Word) or the ‘Normal text’ menu (Docs)
Modify a style once to update all headings
Navigation Pane / Document outline
Heading 1 → Heading 2 → Heading 3
slides.n: A style is a saved set of formatting with a name, such as Normal, Title, Heading 1 and Heading 2. When you apply Heading 1 to every chapter title, three things happen: all chapters look identical, changing the style once updates every heading, and the software understands the document’s structure. That structure powers the Navigation Pane in Word and the document outline in Docs, which let you jump to any section, and it is required for an automatic table of contents. Use Heading 1 for main sections, Heading 2 for subsections and Heading 3 for smaller parts; never skip levels.

slides.h: Page layout: numbers, headers, footers and breaks
b: Ctrl + Enter = page break
Insert → Page Number
Different first page for title pages
Section breaks for different numbering
slides.n: Page numbers are inserted from Insert → Page Number (Word) or Insert → Page numbers (Docs) and update automatically. Headers and footers repeat on every page and usually hold the document title, course code or student name. A page break (Ctrl + Enter) starts a new page cleanly instead of pressing Enter many times. A section break in Word lets different parts of a document have different layouts, for example no page number on the title page, Roman numerals for the contents pages and Arabic numerals from the introduction onward. ‘Different first page’ hides the header on the title page.

slides.h: Table of contents, tables and images

Tables: header row, table styles, alignment
Images: wrap text, keep aspect ratio, captions
Insert → Symbol and Equation for special characters
slides.n: Once headings use styles, insert a table of contents from References → Table of Contents (Word) or Insert → Table of contents (Docs). When headings or page numbers change, click Update Table. Tables organise data in rows and columns: insert them from Insert → Table, add a header row, use table styles and keep tables simple. Images are inserted from Insert → Pictures; set text wrapping (In line with text is safest), resize from the corner to keep proportions and add a caption (References → Insert Caption) such as ‘Figure 1: Bhimber Mart sales chart’. Only use images you have the right to use.

b: Insert Citation and Bibliography (APA, IEEE)
Footnotes
Comments, Track Changes / Suggesting
Share: Viewer, Commenter, Editor

slides.n: Academic writing must credit sources. Word’s References → Insert Citation stores sources and creates a bibliography automatically in styles such as APA or IEEE; Docs offers Tools → Citations. Footnotes add notes at the bottom of a page. For group work, comments let reviewers suggest changes without editing the text, and Track Changes (Word) or Suggesting mode (Docs) records every edit so the author can accept or reject it. Sharing in Docs or OneDrive uses links with Viewer, Commenter or Editor permission. Finally, export to PDF (File → Save As → PDF, or File → Download → PDF) before submitting, so formatting cannot change on another computer.

slides.n: A spreadsheet is a grid that calculates. Shopkeepers use it to track stock, teachers to compile results, accountants to prepare budgets and researchers to analyse survey data. The power of a spreadsheet is that formulas recalculate instantly when any number changes, so you can ask ‘what if?’ questions. In this lecture we build a sales sheet for Bhimber Mart, a fictional store in the main bazaar, and use it to learn the formulas and tools that cover most everyday spreadsheet work.

b: Workbook → Worksheets → Cells
Cell address: column letter + row number (C5)
Range: A1:D10
Formula Bar shows the real content
slides.n: A workbook is the whole file; it contains one or more worksheets (tabs). Each sheet is a grid of columns labelled with letters (A, B, C …) and rows labelled with numbers (1, 2, 3 …). Their intersection is a cell, identified by its address, such as B4. A group of cells is a range, written with a colon, such as B2:B21. Cells hold text (labels), numbers, dates or formulas. The Name Box shows the selected cell’s address and the Formula Bar shows what the cell really contains. Excel is part of Microsoft Office; Google Sheets is free in a browser and saves to Drive automatically.

b: Always start with =
Operators: + - * / ^
Brackets control order: =(B2+C2)/2
Use addresses, not typed numbers
slides.n: Every formula begins with an equals sign. It can use numbers, cell addresses and operators: + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide) and ^ (power). Spreadsheets follow the mathematical order of operations, BODMAS/PEMDAS: brackets first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. So =2+3*4 gives 14 while =(2+3)*4 gives 20. Using cell addresses instead of typed numbers is what makes a spreadsheet useful: =C2*D2 calculates a line total and updates automatically when the price in C2 changes.

b: =SUM(range)  =AVERAGE(range)
=MIN(range)  =MAX(range)
=COUNT(range)  =COUNTA(range)
=COUNTIF(range,condition)
=IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false)
slides.n: A function is a built-in formula with a name and arguments in brackets. SUM adds a range: =SUM(E2:E21). AVERAGE finds the mean, MIN and MAX the smallest and largest values, COUNT counts cells with numbers and COUNTA counts non-empty cells. COUNTIF counts cells meeting a condition, such as =COUNTIF(F2:F21,"Low stock"). IF makes a decision: =IF(D2<10,"Low stock","OK") shows ‘Low stock’ when the quantity is below 10. Text in formulas must be in straight double quotes. Functions can be combined, for example =IF(E2>AVERAGE(E$2:E$21),"Above average","Below").

b: Relative: C2 (changes when copied)
Absolute: $H$1 (always the same cell)
Mixed: $H1 or H$1
F4 toggles reference types
slides.n: When you copy a formula down a column with the fill handle (the small square at the bottom-right of a selected cell), the cell addresses change relative to the new position: =C2*D2 in row 2 becomes =C3*D3 in row 3. This is a relative reference and is usually what you want. Sometimes a formula must always point to one fixed cell, such as a tax rate or discount stored in H1. Add dollar signs to make it absolute: =E2*$H$1. Press F4 in Excel to toggle dollar signs. Mixed references ($H1 or H$1) fix only the column or only the row.

b: Sort A→Z / largest→smallest
Filter to show matching rows
Conditional formatting rules

slides.n: Sorting rearranges rows by a column, for example highest sales first; always select the whole table so rows stay together. Filtering (Data → Filter) shows only rows that meet a condition, such as category ‘Grocery’, without deleting anything. Conditional formatting colours cells automatically, for example red for quantity below 10. Number formats display values as currency (Rs), percentages or dates. Charts turn numbers into pictures: a column or bar chart compares items, a line chart shows change over time and a pie chart shows parts of a whole (use it only for a few categories that add to 100%). Every chart needs a title and labelled axes.

slides.n: Presentations are part of almost every university course, job interview and business meeting. Software makes it easy to fill slides with text, colours and spinning animations, but that is exactly what makes many presentations hard to follow. A slide is a visual aid for a speaker, not a document to be read. In this lecture we learn the tools of PowerPoint and Google Slides, and the design and delivery principles that make an audience listen.

b: Layouts and placeholders
Themes and Slide Master
Normal, Slide Sorter, Slide Show views
Files: .pptx; Slides saves to Drive
slides.n: Microsoft PowerPoint (desktop, web and mobile) and Google Slides (browser, free) both organise a presentation as a sequence of slides. Each slide is built from a layout, such as Title Slide, Title and Content, Two Content or Section Header, which contains placeholders for text, images and charts. A theme applies consistent colours, fonts and backgrounds to all slides. The Slide Master (View → Slide Master) controls the design of every layout at once, for example adding a university logo to all slides. Views include Normal for editing, Slide Sorter for reordering and Slide Show for presenting.
slides.v: Diagram: Presentation development process

b: Contrast, Alignment, Repetition, Proximity
White space
Body text ≥ 28 pt; titles 36–44 pt
One idea per slide; about 6×6 text
slides.n: Good slide design follows a few principles. Contrast: dark text on a light background or the reverse, so it can be read from the back of the room on an old projector. Alignment: line up text and images along invisible edges. Repetition: keep fonts, colours and title positions consistent. Proximity: place related items together. White space: leave empty space so the slide breathes. Use sans-serif fonts such as Calibri, Arial or Segoe UI, at least 28 point for body text and 36–44 for titles. Limit each slide to one main idea and about six lines of text; the ‘6×6 guideline’ suggests no more than six bullets of six words each.

b: Relevant, high-quality, licensed images
Simple charts with a takeaway title
SmartArt / diagrams for processes
Icons for simple concepts
slides.n: People remember pictures better than text. Use high-quality images that support the message, not decoration, and only images you are allowed to use (PowerPoint’s stock images or free licence sources). Charts should be simple: one message per chart, a clear title stating the takeaway such as ‘Grocery sales doubled in Ramadan’, and labels large enough to read. Charts can be inserted from Excel or created in Slides from Sheets. SmartArt (PowerPoint) or diagrams (Slides) show processes, cycles and hierarchies, for example the information processing cycle. Icons can replace words for simple ideas.

b: Transition: between slides (Fade, Push)
Animation: objects on a slide (Appear, Fly in)
Use to reveal steps, not to decorate
Avoid sounds and flashy effects
slides.n: A transition is the effect between slides; an animation moves an object on a slide. Used sparingly, animation can reveal bullets one at a time so the audience listens instead of reading ahead, or show the steps of a process. Overused, it distracts and wastes time. Choose one subtle transition such as Fade for the whole presentation and use animations only when they explain something, for example ‘Appear’ for each step of a flowchart. Avoid sound effects and spinning or bouncing effects in academic presentations.

Rehearse with a timer

slides.n: Speaker notes are written below each slide in the Notes pane and are visible only to the presenter in Presenter View, which also shows the next slide and a timer. Write the points you will say, examples and transitions, so the slide itself can stay short. Rehearse aloud with a timer; a common rule is about one to two minutes per slide. During delivery, face the audience rather than the screen, speak slowly and clearly, point to what matters, and finish with a summary slide and invite questions. Before presenting on another computer, export a PDF backup and embed fonts or use standard ones.

slides.n: Students lose work every semester: a USB drive is left in a computer lab, a phone is stolen, a laptop hard disk fails the night before a deadline. Cloud storage and good file habits prevent almost all of these disasters. In Lecture 1 we met cloud storage as an idea; now we use it properly. We compare the main services, learn to share files safely, design folders that make sense a year later, take organised digital notes and build a backup routine that would survive losing any single device.

b: Google Drive: 15 GB free, Google Workspace integration
OneDrive: 5 GB free, Microsoft Office and Windows integration
Dropbox: 2 GB free, simple sync

slides.n: Google Drive gives 15 GB free shared across Gmail, Drive and Google Photos, and integrates with Docs, Sheets, Slides and Classroom. Microsoft OneDrive gives 5 GB free (more with a Microsoft 365 or university account) and integrates with Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Windows File Explorer. Dropbox gives 2 GB free on its basic plan and is known for simple, reliable sync across devices. All three offer desktop and mobile apps that sync a local folder with the cloud, so a file edited on the lab computer appears on your phone. Free storage limits change over time, so check the provider’s current plan.

slides.h: Sync, version history and offline access
b: Sync keeps devices identical
Version history restores older copies
Offline mode for outages
Bin keeps deleted files for a limited time
slides.n: Sync means keeping the same files identical on several devices and the cloud. When you change a file on one device, the sync client uploads the change and other devices download it. Version history keeps earlier versions so you can restore yesterday’s copy if you overwrite something by mistake: in Google Docs use File → Version history, and in Drive or OneDrive right-click a file → Version history. Files can be made available offline so you can work during internet outages; changes upload when the connection returns. Deleted files go to the Bin/Recycle bin and can usually be restored for about 30 days.

b: Viewer · Commenter · Editor · Owner
Restricted vs organisation vs anyone with link
Least privilege: give minimum access needed
Review and remove access regularly
slides.n: Cloud sharing sends a link instead of a file copy, so everyone sees the latest version. Each person can be given a role: Viewer (can only see), Commenter (can see and comment) or Editor (can change, and by default share). Link sharing can be Restricted (only people added by name), limited to your organisation (for example everyone with a university account) or ‘Anyone with the link’. The safest default is Restricted or ‘Anyone with the link – Viewer’. Never give Editor access to people who do not need it, and remove access when a project ends. Owners can also prevent editors from re-sharing and disable downloading for viewers.

3–4 levels deep

Keep it shallow (three or four levels) and consistent across subjects. A file naming convention makes files easy to sort and find: include what, who and when, avoid spaces and special characters, and use dates in YYYY-MM-DD format so files sort in order. Examples: ICT_Lab03_AliKhan_2026-03-14.docx, ICT_Assignment2_v2_AliKhan.pdf. Avoid names like ‘final final new.docx’.

Evernote: notebooks + tags + search

3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site
slides.n: Microsoft OneNote organises notes into notebooks, sections and pages, like a ring binder; it accepts typed text, handwriting, images, audio and web clippings, and syncs through OneDrive. Evernote organises notes into notebooks and tags and offers powerful search, including text inside images on some plans. Google Keep offers quick notes and checklists. Digital notes are searchable and backed up, but only if you organise them. The 3-2-1 backup rule says: keep 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage (for example laptop and USB drive), with 1 copy off-site (the cloud).

slides.n: When schools and universities closed during the COVID-19 pandemic, Pakistani students experienced online learning on a large scale for the first time. Much of it was improvised, but it showed that ICT can keep education going and open doors to courses far beyond a student’s own campus. Today almost every university uses a Learning Management System, and free platforms offer courses from leading universities. This lecture explains the tools of digital education and the habits a student needs to succeed with them.

slides.n: E-learning is learning supported or delivered through electronic devices and the internet. Synchronous learning happens in real time, such as a live Google Meet class. Asynchronous learning lets students study at their own time, such as recorded lectures, reading material and discussion forums. Blended learning (hybrid) combines face-to-face classes with online activities, for example lectures in class and quizzes on the LMS. A flipped classroom asks students to watch the lecture at home and use class time for problem-solving and discussion. Mobile learning (m-learning) uses phones, which is the main device for many students in Pakistan.

slides.n: A Learning Management System (LMS) is software that delivers, tracks and manages courses. Teachers upload material, create assignments and quizzes, grade work and send announcements; students view content, submit assignments, take quizzes, participate in forums and see their grades. Google Classroom is simple and free with a Google account and links with Drive, Docs and Meet. Moodle is open source and widely used by universities that host it on their own servers; it offers detailed quizzes, forums and gradebooks. Canvas is a commercial LMS with a modern interface used by many international universities. The LMS keeps a record of submission times, which matters for deadlines.

slides.n: A MOOC (Massive Open Online Course) is an online course open to large numbers of learners. Coursera partners with universities and companies; many courses can be audited free, with paid certificates and financial aid available. edX, founded by Harvard and MIT, offers university courses with a similar free audit model. Udemy is a marketplace where instructors sell individual courses, often at heavy discounts. Khan Academy is a non-profit offering free lessons in mathematics, science and computing, with Urdu content for some subjects. Pakistan’s own Virtual University broadcasts lectures and offers degrees through distance learning. When choosing a course, check the instructor, syllabus, reviews, duration and whether the certificate is recognised by employers.

Tools like Kahoot and Quizizz turn revision into live games, Mentimeter collects instant polls, PhET simulations let students experiment with physics virtually and YouTube channels explain topics visually. A virtual classroom recreates a class online with video, chat, whiteboard, screen sharing, breakout rooms and attendance. Research on learning shows that active participation, such as answering questions and practising, improves understanding more than passively watching videos.

slides.n: Three areas of daily life have been changed by ICT more than almost any other for ordinary Pakistani families: health, money and shopping. A grandmother in a village can now consult a doctor by video, a student in Bhimber receives money from home in seconds through a mobile wallet, and a family orders school shoes online with cash on delivery. These services bring convenience but also new risks: health data privacy, fraud calls asking for OTPs and fake online sellers. This lecture covers both the use and the safe use of these tools.

slides.n: Smartphones and wearables such as fitness bands and smartwatches contain sensors: an accelerometer counts steps, a heart-rate sensor measures pulse and GPS records running routes. Apps such as Google Fit, Samsung Health and the Mi Fitness (Zepp) app for Mi Band store this data, show trends and set goals such as 8,000 steps a day. Some devices estimate sleep quality and blood oxygen. These numbers are estimates, useful for motivation and habits but not medical diagnoses. Health data is sensitive personal information, so review which apps can access it and whether it is shared with third parties.

slides.n: Telemedicine delivers healthcare at a distance through video, audio or chat. In Pakistan, Oladoc and Marham let patients search for doctors by speciality and city, read profiles, book in-clinic or online appointments and pay online. Sehat Kahani connects patients, especially in underserved areas, with female doctors through e-clinics and an app. Benefits include saving travel time and cost, access to specialists from small towns and follow-up consultations from home. Limits include the lack of physical examination, the need for stable internet and the risk of unverified ‘doctors’ on social media. Always check that a doctor is registered with the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PM&DC).

slides.n: Mobile wallets such as JazzCash and Easypaisa let users send and receive money, pay utility bills, buy mobile load and pay merchants by QR code, using only a phone number and CNIC-verified account. Internet and mobile banking apps from banks let customers transfer funds, pay bills and check statements. Raast, Pakistan’s instant payment system run by the State Bank of Pakistan, allows free, instant transfers between banks and wallets using a Raast ID, usually the mobile number. Security relies on a PIN, OTPs sent by SMS and device binding. Banks and wallets never ask customers to share their PIN, OTP or full card details by call, SMS or email.

b: Compare prices and read recent reviews
Check seller rating and return policy
Payment: COD, card, wallet, bank transfer
Avoid advance payment to unknown pages
slides.n: E-commerce platforms such as Daraz, Telemart and Shophive sell products from many sellers or their own stock and deliver across Pakistan. Before buying, compare prices, read recent reviews with photos, check the seller’s rating and number of orders, and read the return and warranty policy. Payment options include cash on delivery (COD), cards, wallets and bank transfer. COD reduces the risk of paying for an item that never arrives. Be careful with products advertised only on social media pages that demand advance payment, prices far below market and pressure such as ‘only 2 left’.

b: Never share PIN, OTP, CVV
Check URL and official app
Transaction alerts and app locks
Report to bank helpline and FIA cybercrime
slides.n: Common frauds in Pakistan include calls pretending to be from a bank, wallet or the Benazir Income Support Programme asking for OTPs; fake prize messages; SIM swap attempts; phishing links that copy bank login pages; and fake online shops. Protection rules: never share PIN, OTP or CVV; check the website address and padlock before entering details; enable app locks and biometric login; set SMS alerts for every transaction; use official apps from the Play Store or App Store; and report fraud immediately to your bank’s helpline and block the account or card. Cybercrime can be reported to the FIA’s cybercrime wing.

slides.n: Citizenship means having rights and responsibilities in a community. The internet is now a community we all live in, and digital citizenship means behaving in it safely, respectfully and responsibly. For students, the stakes are real: a photo posted at sixteen can be found by an employer at twenty-five, a cruel comment can deeply hurt a classmate, and a weak password can let someone take over your social media account. This lecture moves from the tools of earlier units to the people who use them.

slides.n: Your digital identity is how you appear online: your names, photos, profiles, posts and the groups you join. Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave. An active footprint is what you deliberately share, such as posts, comments and photos. A passive footprint is collected without you actively posting, such as location history, search history, cookies and app usage. Footprints are persistent (screenshots and archives last), searchable and can be seen by audiences you did not intend, such as future employers, universities and scholarship committees. Search your own name regularly to see what others can find.

slides.n: Online reputation is what others think of you based on your digital footprint. Netiquette (network etiquette) is the set of polite behaviours expected online. Core rules: remember there is a human on the other side; write as you would speak face to face; avoid all capitals, which reads as shouting; respect others’ privacy by not sharing their photos or numbers without permission; check facts before forwarding; keep group chats on topic; respect time zones and working hours when messaging teachers; disagree with ideas, not people. In online classes, use your real name, mute when not speaking and use the chat appropriately.

b: Forms: abuse, rumours, fake profiles, exclusion, stalking
Do not retaliate
Save evidence, block, report
Tell a trusted adult; FIA for serious cases
Bystanders: support and report
slides.n: Cyberbullying is using digital technology to repeatedly threaten, embarrass, insult or exclude someone. Forms include abusive messages, spreading rumours, creating fake profiles, sharing private photos, excluding someone from groups and online stalking. Harassment may also be sexual or blackmail-based. Victims often feel anxious and isolated because the abuse follows them home on their phones. The response steps are: do not reply in anger; take screenshots as evidence with dates; block the person; use the platform’s report tool; tell a trusted adult, teacher or counsellor; and for serious threats or blackmail report to the FIA cybercrime wing. Bystanders should support the victim and report, not share the content.

b: Audience: Friends / private

Review tags; disable post location
Strong, unique passwords or passphrases
Turn on two-step verification
slides.n: Privacy settings control who can see your posts, profile details, friends list and contact information. On Facebook and Instagram, set the audience to Friends or a private account, limit who can find you by phone number, review tagged photos before they appear and turn off location on posts. On WhatsApp, limit who sees profile photo, last seen and about, and who can add you to groups. A strong password is long (at least 12 characters), unique for each important account and not based on personal information; a passphrase of four random words with a number and symbol is easy to remember. Two-step verification (2SV) adds a second check, usually a code from an app or SMS, so a stolen password alone is not enough. A password manager can store unique passwords safely.

Cyberstalking and sharing private images are offences

slides.n: Pakistan’s Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 (PECA) defines cybercrimes and penalties. Offences relevant to students include unauthorised access to someone’s account or data, identity misuse, cyberstalking, spreading sexually explicit images of a person without consent, and spoofing and fraud. The FIA’s cybercrime wing investigates complaints. The law has been amended since its introduction and some provisions are debated, so check current official sources for details. Beyond the law, digital citizens have responsibilities: respect intellectual property, protect others’ privacy and contribute positively, for example by sharing accurate information and helping others learn.

slides.n: Throughout this course you have created documents, spreadsheets, presentations and online content, and you have used material made by others. This final lecture asks ethical questions: who owns digital work, when you may use it, how to give credit and how to avoid spreading false information. These questions matter more each year, as copying is just a right-click away and AI tools can produce text in seconds. We end by launching the Digital Portfolio, which brings together every skill from the course.

b: IP: creations of the mind
Copyright: books, images, music, video, software
Trademark: brand names and logos
Patent: inventions
‘Available online’ ≠ ‘free to use’
slides.n: Intellectual property (IP) is creative work of the mind that the law protects, including writing, music, images, software, inventions and brand names. Copyright protects original creative works such as books, articles, photos, videos, music and code from the moment they are created; the owner has the right to copy, distribute, adapt and display the work. In Pakistan, copyright is governed by the Copyright Ordinance 1962 and IP matters are administered by the Intellectual Property Organisation of Pakistan (IPO-Pakistan). Other IP types include trademarks (brand names and logos) and patents (inventions). Finding an image on Google does not mean it is free to use.

b: Fair use / fair dealing: limited, purpose-based
CC BY · NC · ND · SA · CC0
Always credit: title, author, source, licence
Open media: Wikimedia Commons, Unsplash, Pexels
slides.n: Many copyright laws allow limited use of works without permission for purposes such as criticism, commentary, news reporting, teaching and research, often called fair use or fair dealing. It depends on the purpose, the amount used and the effect on the original’s market, and it is not a blanket permission. Creative Commons (CC) licences let creators give permission in advance. CC BY allows use with credit; NC means non-commercial only; ND means no changes; SA means share adapted works under the same licence. CC0 places work in the public domain. Sources of openly licensed media include Wikimedia Commons, Unsplash and Pexels (check each image’s licence) and Google Images’ ‘Usage rights → Creative Commons licences’ filter.

slides.h: Plagiarism and how to avoid it
b: Types: copy-paste, uncited paraphrase, buying work, self-plagiarism, code copying
Quote + cite
Paraphrase in your own words + cite
Summarise + cite
Reference list in APA/IEEE
slides.n: Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s words, ideas, images or code as your own without proper credit. It includes copying and pasting text, paraphrasing without citation, buying or borrowing assignments, submitting the same work for two courses without permission (self-plagiarism) and copying code. Pakistani universities follow HEC’s plagiarism policy and commonly check work with similarity tools such as Turnitin; penalties range from grade reduction to cancellation of a degree. To avoid plagiarism: quote exact words in quotation marks with a citation; paraphrase by rewriting ideas fully in your own words and structure, still with a citation; summarise main points briefly with a citation; keep notes of sources while researching; and use a consistent citation style such as APA.

b: Follow the course AI policy
Verify facts and references
Disclose AI use when required
Protect personal data
Learn, do not outsource thinking
slides.n: AI writing and image tools can explain concepts, suggest outlines and check grammar, but they can also produce invented facts and references, and submitting AI-generated work as your own may break your institution’s rules. Good practice: check your teacher’s and university’s policy for each assignment; use AI to learn, not to replace your own thinking; verify every fact and reference in an original source; disclose AI assistance when required, for example ‘Grammar checked with an AI tool’; and never enter personal or confidential data into public AI tools. Your own understanding is what will be tested in exams, vivas and jobs.

b: Misinformation · Disinformation · Malinformation
SIFT: Stop, Investigate, Find, Trace
Reverse image search
Check date and official confirmation
Do not forward unverified messages
slides.n: Misinformation is false or misleading information shared without intent to deceive; disinformation is false information spread deliberately; malinformation is true information shared to cause harm. Fake news spreads fast through WhatsApp forwards and social media because it is emotional and surprising. Verify before sharing using the SIFT approach: Stop and check your reaction; Investigate the source; Find better coverage from trusted outlets; Trace claims, quotes and images to the original context. Practical tools include Google reverse image search or Google Lens to find where a photo first appeared, checking the date and checking whether official sources confirm the claim. Be especially careful with health advice, exam leaks and emergency rumours.
